en: Dhātukathā 2 Niddesa 2.10.
The Exposition of the Tenfold Method: The Exposition of the Terms for That Which is Dissociated from What is Dissociated.

Those phenomena that are dissociated from the aggregate of material form (rūpakkhandha), and those phenomena that are dissociated from those [former] phenomena—by how many aggregates, by how many bases (āyatana), and by how many elements (dhātu) are those phenomena dissociated?
Those phenomena are dissociated from four aggregates, from one base, and from seven elements;
they are dissociated from one base and from one element by some [of them].
Those phenomena that are included in the aggregate of feeling;
those phenomena that are included in the aggregate of perception;
those phenomena that are included in the aggregate of mental formations.
Those phenomena that are dissociated from the aggregate of consciousness...
those phenomena that are dissociated from the mind-base (manāyatana)... [and so on]...
those phenomena are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and ten elements.
They are dissociated from one base and from one element by some [factors].
Those phenomena that are [dissociated] from the eye-base …pe… those phenomena that are [dissociated] from the tangible-base …pe…
Those phenomena which are dissociated from the eye-element …pe… those phenomena which are dissociated from the tangible-object-element, and those phenomena which are dissociated from them—
those phenomena are dissociated from four aggregates, one base, and seven elements.
They are dissociated from one base and from one element by some [factors].
Those phenomena associated with the eye-consciousness-element …pe… those phenomena associated with the mind-consciousness-element …
Those phenomena which are dissociated from the truth of the origin,
and those phenomena which are dissociated from those phenomena [of the origin] that are themselves dissociated from the truth of the path—
those phenomena are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and sixteen elements.
They are dissociated from one base and from one element by some [factors].
Those phenomena that are dissociated from the truth of cessation...
those phenomena that are dissociated from the eye-faculty... and so on.
Those phenomena that are dissociated from the body-faculty;
those phenomena that are dissociated from the femininity-faculty;
those phenomena that are dissociated from the masculinity-faculty; and those phenomena that are dissociated from those [aforementioned] phenomena.
Those phenomena are dissociated from four aggregates, one base, and seven elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element by some [of them].
Those phenomena which are dissociated from the mind-faculty (manindriya), those phenomena with which [the former] are dissociated …
Those phenomena are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and ten elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element by some [factors].
Those phenomena which [are associated] with the faculty of pleasure...
Those phenomena that are dissociated from the faculty of pain;
those phenomena that are dissociated from the faculty of mental joy;
those phenomena that are dissociated from the faculty of mental grief; and those phenomena that are dissociated from those [aforementioned] phenomena.
Those states are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and sixteen elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element by some [factors].
Those states which are dissociated from the equanimity faculty—those states with which those [aforementioned] states are dissociated...
Those phenomena are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and eleven elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element by some [of them].
As for those phenomena with the faculty of faith…
Those phenomena [associated] with the faculty of energy … those phenomena [associated] with the faculty of mindfulness … those phenomena [associated] with the faculty of concentration …
Those phenomena by means of the faculty of wisdom … those phenomena by means of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" … those phenomena by means of the faculty of final knowledge …
Those phenomena that are dissociated from the faculty of one who has final knowledge (*aññātāvindriya*);
those phenomena that are dissociated from ignorance (*avijjā*);
those phenomena that are dissociated from the volitional formations conditioned by ignorance (*avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā*); and those phenomena that are dissociated from those [latter] phenomena...
Those states are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and sixteen elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element by some [factors].
As for those states [associated] with consciousness through the condition of volitional formations (saṅkhāra-paccaya) …
Those phenomena which are dissociated from contact by way of the condition of the six sense bases;
those phenomena which are dissociated from those phenomena that are dissociated from feeling by way of the condition of contact—
those phenomena are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and ten elements.
They are dissociated from one base and from one element by some [factors].
Those phenomena which, with feeling as condition, [arise] through craving;
those phenomena which, with craving as condition, [arise] through clinging...
Those phenomena that are dissociated from the kamma-process existence (kammabhava), and those phenomena that are dissociated from those [former] phenomena:
those phenomena are dissociated from one aggregate (khandha), ten bases (āyatana), and sixteen elements (dhātu);
they are dissociated from one base and one element in some respects.

Those phenomena that are dissociated from the fine-material existence (rūpabhava), and those phenomena that are dissociated from those [former] phenomena… those phenomena are dissociated from no aggregates (khandha),
from no bases (āyatana), and from three elements (dhātu). Those phenomena that are dissociated from the non-percipient existence (asaññābhava)…
Those phenomena which are dissociated from the single-aggregate existence...
those phenomena which are dissociated from lamentation, and those phenomena which are dissociated from them...
those phenomena are dissociated from four aggregates, one base, and seven elements.
They are dissociated from one base and from one element by some [factors].
Those phenomena that belong to the formless existence (arūpabhava) … those phenomena that belong to the neither-perception-nor-non-perception existence (nevasaññānāsaññābhava) …
Those phenomena that [arise] through existence consisting of four aggregates...
those phenomena that [arise] through sorrow...
those phenomena that [arise] through suffering...
Those phenomena that [arise] with mental distress...
those phenomena that [arise] with despair...
those phenomena that [arise] with the foundations of mindfulness...
Those phenomena which [are developed] by means of the right exertion...
those phenomena which [are developed] by means of the bases of psychic power...
those phenomena which [are developed] by means of the meditative absorptions...
Those phenomena associated with the immeasurables … those phenomena associated with the five faculties … those phenomena associated with the five powers …
Those phenomena which are dissociated from the seven factors of enlightenment,
those phenomena which are dissociated from the noble eightfold path, and those phenomena which are dissociated from those [latter] phenomena—
those phenomena are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and sixteen elements.
They are dissociated from one base and from one element by some [factors].
Those phenomena which are associated with contact...
those phenomena which are associated with feeling...
Those phenomena associated with perception...
those phenomena associated with volition...
those phenomena associated with consciousness...
Those phenomena which are dissociated from attention, and those phenomena which are dissociated from those [other] phenomena:
those phenomena are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and ten elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element with respect to some [phenomena].
Those states that are dissociated from resolve, and those states that are dissociated from those [latter] states:
those states are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and fifteen elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element with respect to some [factors].
2.10.1. Triplets:
Those states which are dissociated from wholesome states;
those states which are dissociated from unwholesome states; those states which are dissociated from those [unwholesome] states.
Those states are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and sixteen elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element with respect to certain [other] states.
Those states which are associated with states associated with pleasant feeling...
Those phenomena which are dissociated from the phenomena associated with painful feeling, and those phenomena which are dissociated from those [first] phenomena—
those phenomena are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and fifteen elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element in some respects.
Those phenomena which are dissociated from the phenomena associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, and those phenomena which are dissociated from those [former] phenomena:
these phenomena are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and eleven elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element in some respects.
Those phenomena which are dissociated from resultant phenomena, and those phenomena which are dissociated from those [resultant] phenomena:
those phenomena are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and ten elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element with respect to some [phenomena].
Those phenomena which are dissociated from phenomena that are of the nature to ripen,
and those phenomena which are dissociated from phenomena that are defiled and subject to defilement—
those phenomena are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and sixteen elements.
They are dissociated from one base (āyatana) and from one element (dhātu),
and from certain [factors]. Those factors which are dissociated from those factors that are neither-result-nor-cause-of-result,
and those factors which are dissociated from those factors that are not-clung-to-but-object-of-clinging, [are dissociated] from those factors...
Those phenomena are dissociated from none of the aggregates, none of the bases, and five of the elements.
Those phenomena which are dissociated from phenomena that are neither-clung-to-nor-liable-to-clinging,
and those phenomena which are dissociated from phenomena that are neither-afflicted-nor-afflicting— those phenomena are dissociated from those [other] phenomena.
Those states are dissociated from none of the aggregates, from none of the bases, and from six elements.
Those states which are dissociated from states accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought—those states which are dissociated from those states [are as follows]:
those states are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and fifteen elements.
They are dissociated from one base and from one element, and from certain [factors].
Those factors which are dissociated from states that are without applied thought but with sustained thought;
those factors which are dissociated from states accompanied by rapture; and those factors which are dissociated from those [latter] states...
Those states are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and sixteen elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element by some [factors].
Those states which are dissociated from states that are without applied thought and sustained thought (*avitakka-avicāra*), those states are dissociated from those states...
Those phenomena are dissociated from none of the aggregates, from none of the bases, and from one element.
Those phenomena which are dissociated from the phenomena associated with pleasure, and those phenomena which are dissociated from those [former] phenomena—
those phenomena are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and fifteen elements.
They are dissociated from one base and from one element,
and from some [other] factors. Those factors which are dissociated from the factors associated with equanimity, and those factors which are dissociated from those [former] factors—
those factors are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and eleven elements.
They are dissociated from one base and from one element by some [factors].
Those factors which are dissociated from states to be abandoned by seeing;
those factors which are dissociated from states to be abandoned by cultivation...
Those phenomena which [are associated] with phenomena whose roots are to be abandoned by vision;
those phenomena which [are associated] with phenomena whose roots are to be abandoned by cultivation;
those phenomena which [are associated] with phenomena leading to accumulation...
Those phenomena which [are related] to the phenomena leading to diminution;
those phenomena which [are related] to the phenomena of the trainee (sekha);
those phenomena which [are related] to the phenomena of the adept (asekha).
Those states which are dissociated from sublime states, and those states which are dissociated from those [sublime] states:
those states are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and sixteen elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element in some respects.
Those phenomena which are dissociated from immeasurable phenomena... those phenomena which are dissociated from sublime phenomena...
those phenomena which are dissociated from those [sublime] phenomena are dissociated from none of the aggregates, none of the bases, and six elements. –12
Those states which are dissociated from states having limited objects, and those states which are dissociated from those [limited] states:
those states are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and ten elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element with respect to some [of them].
Those states which [arise] through states with exalted objects;
those states which [arise] through states with immeasurable objects;
those states which [arise] through inferior states.
Those phenomena which [arise] through phenomena fixed in wrongness;
those phenomena which [arise] through phenomena fixed in rightness;
those phenomena which [arise] through phenomena having the Path as their object...
Those phenomena which are dissociated from phenomena having the Path as their cause,
those phenomena which are dissociated from phenomena having the Path as their dominant influence, and those phenomena which are dissociated from those [latter] phenomena—
those phenomena are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and sixteen elements.
They are dissociated from one base and from one element,
and from some [other factors]. Those phenomena that are dissociated from unarisen phenomena, and those phenomena that are dissociated from those [unarisen] phenomena—
those phenomena are dissociated from none of the aggregates, from none of the bases, and from five elements.
Those states which are dissociated from states having past objects,
and those states which are dissociated from states having future objects—
those states are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and sixteen elements.
They are dissociated from one base and from one element by some [factors].
Those phenomena which [are dissociated] from phenomena having present objects;
those phenomena which [are dissociated] from phenomena having internal objects...
Those states which are dissociated from states having external objects...
those states which are dissociated from states having both internal and external objects...
those states are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and ten elements.
They are dissociated from one base and from one element by some [factors].
Those factors which are dissociated from visible and impinging phenomena;
those factors which are dissociated from invisible and impinging phenomena; those factors which are dissociated from those [invisible and impinging] factors...
Those states are dissociated from four aggregates, one base, and seven elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element by some [of their factors].
2.10.2. Duka (Pairs)
2.10.2.1. Group on Causes (Hetugocchaka):
Those phenomena which [arise] with causal phenomena...
those phenomena which [arise] with phenomena possessing causes...
Those phenomena that [arise] with phenomena associated with roots;
those phenomena that [arise] with both roots and root-possessing phenomena;
those phenomena that [arise] with root-possessing phenomena that are not themselves roots.
Those phenomena which are dissociated from those phenomena that are both roots and associated with roots;
those phenomena which are dissociated from those phenomena that are associated with roots but are not themselves roots;
and those phenomena which are dissociated from those phenomena that are neither roots nor accompanied by roots...
Those states are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and sixteen elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element by some [of their factors].
2.10.2.2. The Short Intermediate Dyad.
Those phenomena that [arise] with respect to phenomena that are not conditions;
those phenomena that [arise] with respect to unconditioned phenomena;
those phenomena that [arise] with respect to visible phenomena...
Those phenomena which are dissociated from phenomena that possess resistance,
those phenomena which are dissociated from material phenomena, and those phenomena which are dissociated from those [latter] phenomena—
those phenomena are dissociated from four aggregates, one base, and seven elements.
They are dissociated from one base and from one element, and from some [factors].
Those factors which are dissociated from supramundane states, and those factors which are dissociated from them...
those factors are dissociated from none of the aggregates, from none of the bases, and from six elements.
2.10.2.3. The Group on the Taints (Āsavagocchaka):
Those phenomena which [arise] with the taints as their condition...
those phenomena which [arise] with phenomena associated with the taints as their condition...
Those phenomena which are dissociated from those phenomena that are both taints (*āsava*) and subject to taints (*sāsava*);
those phenomena which are dissociated from those phenomena that are both taints and associated with taints;
and those phenomena which are dissociated from those phenomena that are associated with taints but are not themselves taints.
Those states are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and sixteen elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element with respect to certain [states].
Those states which are dissociated from the untainted (anāsava) states...

Those states which are dissociated from those states that are dissociated from the taintless (anāsava) states and dissociated from the outflows (āsava)—those states are dissociated from none of the aggregates (khandha), none of the bases (āyatana), and six elements (dhātu).
2.10.2.4–9. The Group on Fetters (saṃyojana-gocchaka), etc.
Those phenomena which, by way of the fetters...
those phenomena which, by way of the ties...
those phenomena which, by way of the floods... [are associated with them].
Those phenomena which [are opposed] to the factors of enlightenment;
those phenomena which [are opposed] to the hindrances;
those phenomena which [are opposed] to the perversions.
Those phenomena which are dissociated from those phenomena associated with misapprehension (*parāmāsa-saṃpayutta*);
those phenomena which are dissociated from both the misapprehensions and the phenomena misapprehended by them;
those phenomena which are dissociated from those [latter] phenomena—those phenomena are dissociated from one aggregate (*khandha*), ten bases (*āyatana*), and sixteen elements (*dhātu*).
They are dissociated from one base and from one element by way of some [factors].

Those factors which are dissociated from factors that are not adhered to—those factors which are dissociated from factors dissociated from the taints (āsava) and not adhered to—from those factors, those [other] factors are dissociated. …
Those states are dissociated from none of the aggregates, none of the bases, and six elements.
2.10.2.10. The Group on Fetters (Saṃyojanagocchaka), etc.:
Those states which [are dissociated] from states that possess an object...
Those phenomena which [are associated] with mental states;
those phenomena which [are associated] with mental factors;
those phenomena which [are associated] with states associated with consciousness.
Those phenomena [conditioned] by phenomena associated with mind;
those phenomena [conditioned] by phenomena associated with and originated by mind;
those phenomena [conditioned] by phenomena associated with, originated by, and co-existent with mind.
Those phenomena which are dissociated from those phenomena that are conjoined with, originated by, and follow upon the mind—
those phenomena are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and ten elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element in some respects.
Those phenomena that [arise] with phenomena that are objectless;
those phenomena that [arise] with phenomena dissociated from consciousness;
those phenomena that [arise] with phenomena disconnected from consciousness.
Those phenomena which are dissociated from the states that are subject to clinging, and those phenomena which are dissociated from those [former] states—
those phenomena are dissociated from four aggregates, one base, and seven elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element with respect to some [of them].
Those phenomena which are dissociated from phenomena not associated with clinging—those phenomena which are dissociated from those phenomena...
those phenomena are dissociated from none of the aggregates, none of the bases, and five elements.
2.10.2.11–12. The Group on Clinging, etc.
Those phenomena which [arise] from phenomena that are objects of clinging;
those phenomena which [arise] from phenomena that are defilements;
those phenomena which [arise] from phenomena that are afflicted.
Those phenomena which [arise] together with defiled states;
those phenomena which [arise] together with both defilements and defiling states;
those phenomena which [arise] together with both defilements and defiled states.
Those phenomena which are dissociated from phenomena that are both defiled and not themselves defilements;
those phenomena which are dissociated from phenomena that are both defilements and associated with defilements;

those phenomena which are dissociated from phenomena that are associated with defilements but are not themselves defilements; and those phenomena which are dissociated from those [aforementioned] phenomena.
Those states are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and sixteen elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element by some [of them].
Those states which are dissociated from non-defiled states...
Those phenomena which are dissociated from those phenomena that are dissociated from defilements and are non-defiled—those phenomena which are dissociated from those [latter] phenomena...
those phenomena are dissociated from none of the aggregates, none of the bases, and six elements.
2.10.2.13. Piṭṭhiduka (The Subsequent Pair)
Those states which [are associated] with states to be abandoned by vision;
those states which [are associated] with states to be abandoned by cultivation;
those states which [are associated] with states whose roots are to be abandoned by vision.
Those phenomena which are dissociated from those phenomena whose roots are to be abandoned by cultivation—
those [latter] phenomena are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and sixteen elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element with respect to some [of them].

Those phenomena which are dissociated from those phenomena that possess applied thought (*savitakka*), and those phenomena which are dissociated from those phenomena that possess sustained thought (*savicāra*)—
those phenomena are dissociated from one aggregate (*khandha*), ten bases (*āyatana*), and fifteen elements (*dhātu*).
They are dissociated from one base and from one element, and from certain [other] factors.
Those factors which are dissociated from factors without initial application (*avitakka*),
those factors which are dissociated from factors without sustained application (*avicāra*), and those factors which are dissociated from those [latter] factors...
Those states are dissociated from none of the aggregates, from none of the bases, and from one element.

Those states which are dissociated from states accompanied by rapture, those states which are dissociated from states conjoined with rapture, and those states which are dissociated from those [latter] states...
Those phenomena are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and sixteen elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element by some [of them].
Those phenomena which are dissociated from the phenomena associated with pleasure, those phenomena are dissociated from those [same] phenomena …
Those states are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and fifteen elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element with respect to some [states].
Those states which are dissociated from states associated with equanimity—those states are dissociated from those states...
Those states are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and eleven elements;
they are dissociated from one base and one element by some [factors].
They are not dissociated from states belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). Those states which...
Those states which are dissociated from states that are not included [in the mundane],
those states which are dissociated from states that are unsurpassed—
those states are dissociated from none of the aggregates, none of the bases, and six elements.
Those phenomena which [arise] with fine-material-sphere phenomena as their condition;
those phenomena which [arise] with immaterial-sphere phenomena as their condition;
those phenomena which [arise] with leading-out phenomena as their condition.
Those phenomena that are dissociated from those phenomena which are determined,
and those phenomena which are dissociated from those phenomena which have a refuge— by how many aggregates, by how many bases, and by how many elements are those phenomena dissociated?
Those phenomena are dissociated from one aggregate, ten bases, and sixteen elements.
They are dissociated from one base and from one element by some [factors].
The dhammāyatana and the dhammadhātu,
as well as the truth of suffering and life-faculty;
The six sense bases, name-and-form,
the four great elements,
birth, aging, and death.
There are nineteen in the Tika sections,
fifty in the Gocchaka sections,
and eight words in the Cūḷantara section.
Fifteen in the middle section,
eighteen thereafter;
this [portion] consists of two hundred and thirty-three words.
"It is not obtained in association.
[123] The tenth is the exposition of the term "dissociated" regarding that which is dissociated.
